title: Roundtree v. City of Page
description: Whether an initiative proposed by residents of the City of Page, which seeks to prevent the narrowing of a specific street, is legislative in nature and thus falls within the citizens' right to initiate laws at the local level, or if it is administrative and therefore not subject to citizen initiative.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the proposed initiative is legislative because it seeks to enact a permanent rule, creates policy, and therefore falls within the constitutional authority of the City's electors to initiate laws.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the proposed initiative is administrative, not legislative, because it merely implements or attempts to control an already established City policy (the Streetscape Project) and would supplant the city engineer's delegated administrative authority.
decision_outcome: The Arizona Supreme Court vacated the decision of the court of appeals and reversed the decision of the trial court, remanding the case to allow the Committee's initiative to proceed to the ballot.

title: Smith v. Fontes
description: Whether A.R.S. § 19-121.04(A), which mandates double counting of some invalid signatures, unconstitutionally raises the 15% signature threshold for constitutional initiatives, thereby hindering the right to place initiatives on the ballot.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs (and legislative leaders) argued that A.R.S. § 19-121.04(A) does not violate the constitution, or that any increase in the signature threshold due to its application was negligible.
defendant_argument: The defendant (Make Elections Fair PAC) argued that A.R.S. § 19-121.04(A) is unconstitutional as applied because its double counting mechanism effectively raised the 15% signature threshold, requiring more signatures than constitutionally mandated.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's judgment dismissing the challenge to the Initiative, ruling that A.R.S. § 19-121.04(A) is unconstitutional as applied because it impermissibly raised the 15% signature threshold for constitutional initiatives.

title: Knight v. Fontes
description: Whether the geographic voting districts for the retention election process of court of appeals judges, as set forth in A.R.S. § 12-120.02, violate the Free and Equal Elections Clause and the Equal Privileges and Immunities Clause of the Arizona Constitution, with plaintiffs arguing they do and defendants arguing they do not.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that § 12-120.02 unconstitutionally disenfranchises Arizona voters and gives unequal weight to their votes by limiting participation in court of appeals judge retention elections to specific geographic districts, rather than allowing statewide participation for judges with statewide jurisdiction.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that § 12-120.02 is constitutional, does not violate the Free and Equal Elections Clause or the Equal Privileges and Immunities Clause, and that the one-person, one-vote principle does not apply to judicial elections.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the superior court's order dismissing the plaintiffs' claim, concluding that A.R.S. § 12-120.02 does not violate the Free and Equal Elections Clause or the Equal Privileges and Immunities Clause of the Arizona Constitution.

title: Sync Title Agency, LLC v. Arizona Corporation Commission
description: Whether Sync Title Agency, LLC, is liable for selling unregistered securities and committing securities fraud, with the plaintiff arguing for a non-public offering exemption and against fraud findings, and the defendant arguing against the exemption and for the fraud findings.
plaintiff_argument: Sync argued that the sale of membership interest was an exempt non-public offering, that it had a constitutional right to a jury trial for alleged securities fraud violations, and that the Commission's findings of securities fraud were not supported by substantial evidence.
defendant_argument: The Arizona Corporation Commission argued that Sync sold an unregistered, non-exempt security and committed securities fraud through misrepresentations and omissions, and that Arizona law does not grant a jury-trial right for Commission enforcement actions.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed in part, vacating the Commission's order in part, and remanded the case for proceedings consistent with its decision. It found Sync participated in the sale, denied a jury trial right, but concluded the offering was exempt from registration. It also found some fraud claims were puffery or had a reasonable basis, but upheld the fraud finding regarding the personal use of investment funds.

title: Francisco v. Affiliated Urologists
description: Whether an FDA black box warning can substitute for expert testimony to establish the standard of care in medical malpractice cases under Arizona law.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that expert testimony was not necessary because a jury could understand the FDA black box warnings and determine their materiality, and that requiring such testimony unconstitutionally abrogated their right to sue as they could not find an expert.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that expert medical testimony is required to establish the standard of care in medical malpractice claims, and FDA black box warnings alone are insufficient to meet this requirement.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the court of appeals' memorandum decision and affirmed the trial court's judgment, which had dismissed the plaintiffs' claim for failure to provide a preliminary expert opinion affidavit.

title: Gilpin v. Harris
description: Whether defendants adjudicated 'guilty except insane' (GEI) are criminally responsible for their actions and thus liable for victim restitution.
plaintiff_argument: Lisa Gilpin, as a victim, argued that Marcos Martinez, a GEI defendant, should pay restitution under Arizona's Victims' Bill of Rights, asserting that GEI defendants are criminally responsible.
defendant_argument: Marcos Martinez argued that a GEI judgment is not a 'conviction' for restitution purposes, and therefore restitution was unavailable, relying on the precedent set in State v. Heartfield.
decision_outcome: The court overruled the precedent set in State v. Heartfield and held that restitution is available from defendants adjudged 'guilty except insane' when their actions caused or threatened death or serious injury, remanding the case for further proceedings.

title: Gilmore v. Gallego
description: Whether "release time" provisions in a memorandum of understanding (MOU) between the City of Phoenix and a union violate free-speech, free-association, right-to-work rights, or the Gift Clause of the Arizona Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the release time provisions violate their free-speech, free-association, and right-to-work rights, and also violate the Gift Clause, especially if the City pays for it.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the release time provisions do not violate free-speech, free-association, or right-to-work rights because the City pays for them, and do not violate the Gift Clause because they serve a public purpose and are supported by adequate consideration.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the release time provisions do not violate free-speech, free-association, or right-to-work rights, but they do violate the Gift Clause of the Arizona Constitution, remanding the case for judgment in favor of the Employees on the Gift Clause claim.

title: Pima County. v. State
description: Whether the State must reimburse Pima County for desegregation expenses that exceed the Arizona Constitution's 1% Limit on residential property taxes as "additional state aid for education" following the 2018 legislative amendments to A.R.S. § 15-910, and whether these taxes continue to be "primary property taxes" eligible for reimbursement.
plaintiff_argument: The State must reimburse Pima County for desegregation expenses because the 2018 amendments to § 15-910 are unworkable, do not trump constitutional limitations, and do not eliminate the State's reimbursement obligation for primary property taxes.
defendant_argument: The State is not obligated to reimburse Pima County because the 2018 amendments reclassified desegregation expenses as a new type of secondary property tax, which is not eligible for state reimbursement under § 15-972(E), and these amendments are constitutional.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the State is not obligated to reimburse Pima County for desegregation expenses, affirming the court of appeals' opinion.

title: Mitchell v. Palmer
description: Whether the Maricopa County Attorney's Office (MCAO) should be disqualified from prosecuting Tamira Durand's case because one of its employees is a victim in the case, with the State arguing against disqualification and Durand arguing for it.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the victim-employee's conflict was not imputed to the entire office, there was no appearance of impropriety, and their screening procedure was adequate to avoid conflict, thus disqualification was unwarranted.
defendant_argument: Durand argued that her due process rights would be violated if prosecuted by an agency with a conflict of interest, asserting that the victim-employee's involvement could lead to pressure for a less favorable plea offer or force the case to trial.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the trial court's order disqualifying the Maricopa County Attorney's Office and remanded the case for reconsideration, instructing the trial court to apply the Gomez factors and consider Durand's due process rights and the victim's rights.

title: Neptune Swimming Foundation v. City of Scottsdale
description: Whether the City of Scottsdale violated the Gift Clause by not considering a higher bid when awarding a license and whether it abused its discretion by canceling a Request for Proposal (RFP) process.
plaintiff_argument: Neptune argued the City violated the Gift Clause by awarding a license at below-market rates and abused its discretion by canceling the RFP and not awarding the license to Neptune, the most advantageous bidder.
defendant_argument: The City argued it did not violate the Gift Clause, as a higher bid is not conclusive for fair market value, and it did not abuse its discretion by canceling the RFP and extending an existing license.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed summary judgment for the City on the Gift Clause claim, finding no violation, but reversed summary judgment for the City on the procurement code claim, remanding for further proceedings to determine if the City abused its discretion.

title: Cao v. PFP Dorsey Investments
description: Whether the Arizona Condominium Act, specifically § 33-1228(C), permits a condominium association to force the sale of individual units rather than the entire condominium property upon termination, with the plaintiffs arguing it requires the sale of all property and the defendants arguing it allows for the sale of less than all.
plaintiff_argument: The Xias argued that the forced sale of their unit violated § 33-1228(C) because it prohibited the forced sale of less than an entire condominium, and alternatively, that § 33-1228 was unconstitutional as it authorized a taking of private property for private use. They also contended that the 2018 amendments to the statute should not apply without separate consent.
defendant_argument: The Association and PFP Dorsey argued that the forced sale of the Xias' unit complied with § 33-1228, implying that the statute allowed for the sale of less than an entire condominium, and that the 2018 version of the statute was applicable.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's dismissal of the eminent domain claim but reversed the court of appeals' interpretation of § 33-1228(C), holding that the statute required the sale of all condominium property, not just individual units, if any property was to be sold upon termination. The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with this opinion, and the court also ruled that the 2018 version of the statute applied.

title: State v. Santillanes
description: Whether the State has the right to appeal a trial court's order granting expungement and restoration of civil rights, or whether it may seek relief only through a petition for special action.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued it has the right to appeal expungement orders under A.R.S. § 13-4032(4) because such orders affect its substantial rights.
defendant_argument: Santillanes argued that A.R.S. § 36-2862(F) provides the exclusive grounds for appeal in expungement cases, allowing only petitioners to appeal denials, and that an expungement order does not affect the State's substantial rights.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the State has the right to appeal an order expunging records pertaining to a felony conviction and restoring civil rights under A.R.S. § 13-4032(4), vacating parts of the court of appeals' opinion and remanding for further proceedings.

title: Planned Parenthood of Arizona v. Hazelrigg
description: Whether the Arizona Legislature repealed or otherwise restricted A.R.S. § 13-3603, a near-total abortion ban, by enacting later abortion statutes in Title 36, specifically A.R.S. § 36-2322, which proscribes physicians from performing elective abortions after fifteen weeks' gestation.
plaintiff_argument: Planned Parenthood argued that § 36-2322 implicitly authorizes abortions up to fifteen weeks and should be harmonized with § 13-3603, effectively repealing or restricting the older, near-total ban.
defendant_argument: The Attorney General and intervenors argued that § 36-2322 merely restricted abortion within the confines of Roe v. Wade and did not repeal § 13-3603, which became enforceable after Roe was overturned.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's judgment vacating the injunction of § 13-3603, making the near-total abortion ban enforceable, and vacated the court of appeals' opinion, with a temporary stay on enforcement for fourteen days.

title: Torres v. Jai Dining Services
description: Whether the anti-abrogation clause extends to dram-shop actions recognized after statehood, thereby preventing the legislature from limiting such actions.
plaintiff_argument: The anti-abrogation clause protects the common law dram-shop action, which evolved from pre-statehood negligence rights, and thus the legislature cannot limit it.
defendant_argument: The anti-abrogation clause does not protect dram-shop actions because they were created after statehood, allowing the legislature to limit them.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the anti-abrogation clause does not protect dram-shop actions because they were recognized after statehood, thus affirming the legislature's ability to limit such actions and ruling in favor of JAI Dining Services.

title: Draper v. Gentry
description: Whether a defendant must satisfy a 'reasonable possibility' or 'substantial probability' standard to compel the extraction of GPS data from a crime victim's vehicle for their defense, balancing the defendant's right to a complete defense against the victim's constitutional and statutory privacy rights.
plaintiff_argument: Lane Draper argued that compelling the extraction of GPS data from his truck violated his constitutional rights against unreasonable search and seizure (Fourth Amendment), his state constitutional privacy rights, and his rights as a victim under the Victims' Bill of Rights.
defendant_argument: Jordon Nez argued that his due process right to present a complete defense, including a third-party defense implicating Draper, required access to Draper's GPS data, and that the 'reasonable possibility' standard should apply.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the trial court's order and remanded the case, establishing a conditional standard for compelling GPS data extraction from a crime victim's vehicle, requiring a 'reasonable possibility' for in-camera review with safeguards and a 'substantial probability' for direct disclosure.

title: State v. Purcell
description: Whether the court of appeals had appellate jurisdiction over the dismissal of resentencing proceedings for juvenile offenders, with petitioners arguing for jurisdiction based on affected substantial rights and the state arguing against it, characterizing the proceedings as non-appealable post-conviction relief.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners argued that the resentencing proceedings were not post-conviction relief (PCR) proceedings, and the trial court's orders dismissing them affected their substantial rights, thus granting the court of appeals jurisdiction under A.R.S. § 13-4033(A)(3).
defendant_argument: The state argued that the court of appeals lacked jurisdiction because the superior court's decision was a final decision in a post-conviction relief proceeding, which is not an appealable order and requires a petition for review under Rule 32.16(a)(1).
decision_outcome: The Arizona Supreme Court concluded that the court of appeals had jurisdiction over the appeals in these cases and remanded the cases to the court of appeals for consideration of the issues presented.

title: State v. Brearcliffe
description: Whether a defendant's constitutional right to appeal can be divested under A.R.S. § 13-4033(C) without prior notice and an opportunity at sentencing to prove their absence was involuntary.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that Johnson waived his right to appeal by absconding and that the statute does not require an express finding of involuntary absence by the trial court.
defendant_argument: Johnson argued that he was not afforded the opportunity to prove his absence was involuntary and that § 13-4033(C) is unconstitutional as a procedural law usurping the Court's rulemaking authority.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the court of appeals' order and remanded the case to the trial court to provide Johnson an opportunity to prove by clear and convincing evidence that his absence was involuntary.

title: Matthews v. The Industrial Commission of Arizona
description: Whether A.R.S. § 23-1043.01(B), which limits workers' compensation claims for mental illnesses to those arising from an "unexpected, unusual or extraordinary stress" situation, violates article 18, section 8 of the Arizona Constitution or the equal protection guarantee of article 2, section 13.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that A.R.S. § 23-1043.01(B) unconstitutionally restricts workers' compensation for mental injuries by treating them differently than physical injuries, violating Article 18, Section 8 of the Arizona Constitution and equal protection guarantees.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that A.R.S. § 23-1043.01(B) is constitutional because the original Workers' Compensation Act did not encompass mental injuries, and the legislature has the prerogative to define and expand workers' compensation coverage within limits.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the decision of the court of appeals, upholding the constitutionality of A.R.S. § 23-1043.01(B) and affirming the ALJ's award determination that the plaintiff's mental injury claim was non-compensable.

title: Burns v. Arizona Public Service Co.
description: Whether the Arizona Constitution allows a majority of commissioners to prevent an individual commissioner from exercising investigatory powers and whether an aggrieved commissioner has standing to seek judicial recourse.
plaintiff_argument: Robert Burns argued that individual commissioners have constitutional and statutory authority to inspect and investigate public service corporation records and affairs, compel testimony and evidence via subpoena, and have standing to seek declaratory relief when their investigatory efforts are impeded.
defendant_argument: Arizona Public Service Company and the Arizona Corporation Commission argued that the Commission as a whole controls investigatory powers, especially in ratemaking cases, and can quash individual subpoenas, and that Burns lacked standing or failed to exhaust administrative remedies.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the court of appeals' opinion, reversed the superior court's denial of summary judgment, and remanded the case, ruling that a majority of commissioners cannot prevent an individual commissioner from exercising investigatory powers and that an aggrieved commissioner has standing to seek declaratory judgment.

title: Leibsohn v. Hobbs
description: Whether signatures collected by initiative petition circulators should be disqualified for failing to strictly comply with statutory registration requirements regarding residence address unit numbers and the submission of multiple affidavits.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that signatures should be disqualified because circulators failed to strictly comply with statutory requirements by not listing unit numbers in multi-unit housing addresses and not submitting a new affidavit for each initiative petition.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that a unit number is not explicitly required in a residence address and that one affidavit should suffice for multiple initiatives, further asserting that the Secretary of State's registration procedures made strict compliance with the affidavit requirement impossible.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's judgment, ruling that a unit number is not required in a circulator's residence address and declining to disqualify signatures for noncompliance with the multiple affidavit requirement because the Secretary's procedures made compliance impossible, thereby protecting the constitutional right to the initiative process.

title: Arizona Free Enterprise Club v. Hobbs
description: Whether tax revenue measures, specifically Senate Bill 1828, are exempt from the people's referendum power under the Arizona Constitution, with the plaintiff arguing for exemption and the defendant arguing against it.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that SB 1828 is exempt from referendum because the Arizona Constitution exempts laws for the support and maintenance of state departments and institutions, and SB 1828 falls under this exemption.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that SB 1828 is subject to referendum because it does not qualify as a "support and maintenance" measure that appropriates state funds or generates necessary revenue, and that only revenue-increasing measures should be exempt.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the trial court's decision, ruling that Senate Bill 1828, a tax revenue measure, is exempt from the referendum process.

title: Fann v. Kemp
description: Whether legislative privilege protects communications related to an election audit from public disclosure, with the plaintiff arguing against such protection and the defendant arguing for it.
plaintiff_argument: American Oversight argued that the audit communications are public records subject to disclosure, not protected by legislative privilege, especially if administrative or political, or if the privilege was waived.
defendant_argument: The Arizona Senate argued that the audit communications are protected by legislative privilege because the audit was a legitimate legislative activity within the legislature's authority to investigate and propose legislation, and the privilege was not waived.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the trial court's order to disclose all communications concerning the Audit, vacated the court of appeals' opinion, and remanded the case for the trial court to resolve the Senate's legislative privilege claims consistent with the Supreme Court's broader interpretation of legislative privilege.

title: Willis v. Bernini
description: Whether a person under grand jury investigation has a due process right to a fair and impartial presentation of clearly exculpatory evidence, and whether a prosecutor has a duty to present such evidence, including evidence relevant to a justification defense, to a grand jury.
plaintiff_argument: Willis argued that the State withheld clearly exculpatory evidence of a justification defense, which it was obligated to present even without a specific request.
defendant_argument: The State contended it complied with its obligations, did not withhold exculpatory evidence, and asserted there is no constitutional due process right to a fair and impartial presentation of evidence before a grand jury.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the trial court's ruling concerning Willis' 12.9 Motion and remanded the case with instructions to send it back to the grand jury for a redetermination of probable cause.

title: State v. Robinson
description: Whether Dwandarrius Jamar Robinson's convictions and death sentences should be affirmed, considering his challenges to the trial court's denial of Batson challenges, findings of aggravating circumstances, and the life imprisonment instruction.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that its peremptory strikes were race-neutral, the jury's findings of especially cruel, heinous, or depraved murder were supported by substantial evidence, and the life imprisonment instruction accurately stated the law.
defendant_argument: Robinson argued that the trial court erred in denying his Batson challenges, that the aggravating circumstances were not proven, and that the life imprisonment instruction was legally flawed, all of which denied him a fair trial and due process.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Robinson's convictions and sentences.

title: State v. Reed
description: Whether a victim's attorney fees are recoverable as criminal restitution and, if so, to what extent.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the attorney fees were a direct result of Reed's criminal conduct and thus properly ordered as restitution.
defendant_argument: The petitioners argued that the attorney fees were consequential damages, not directly caused by Reed's criminal conduct, and therefore not recoverable as restitution.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the trial court's restitution order for most of C.C.'s attorney fees, finding them to be indirect consequential damages, but remanded for a determination on two specific billing entries.

title: Arizona School Boards Association,  Inc. v. State
description: Whether four legislative budget reconciliation bills (HB 2898, SB 1824, SB 1825, and SB 1819) violate the Arizona Constitution's "title requirement" or "single subject rule."
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that all four budget reconciliation bills violated the title requirement, and that SB 1819 also violated the single subject rule, rendering them unconstitutional.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the budget reconciliation bills' titles satisfied the title requirement, that the bills complied with constitutional standards, and that the plaintiffs lacked standing to challenge SB 1819, presenting a non-justiciable political question.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's judgment, ruling that the challenged sections of HB 2898, SB 1824, SB 1825, and SB 1819 violated the title requirement and that SB 1819 entirely violated the single subject rule, rendering those sections and SB 1819 unconstitutional and void.

title: Fay v. Fox
description: Whether a crime victim has a constitutional and statutory right to be heard on the merits of a defendant's motion for a delayed appeal of a restitution order, with the plaintiff arguing for this right and the defendant arguing against it.
plaintiff_argument: Beth Fay argued that she has a constitutional and statutory right to be heard on Hanson's motion for a delayed appeal of the restitution order because it implicates her rights to due process, prompt restitution, and finality, and could delay or extinguish her restitution award.
defendant_argument: Jordan Michael Hanson argued that Fay, as a victim, does not have a right to be heard on his motion for a delayed appeal of the restitution order, as victims are not 'parties' in such proceedings and his right to a delayed appeal, if not his fault, should prevail without victim intervention.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the court of appeals decision and reversed the trial court judgment, ruling that a crime victim has a constitutional and statutory right to be heard on the merits of a defendant's motion for a delayed appeal of a restitution order.

title: Fann v. State
description: Whether Proposition 208, a voter initiative imposing an income tax surcharge for education funding, violates the Education Expenditure Clause by purporting to exempt its funds from expenditure limitations and whether it violates the Tax Enactment Clause by imposing a new tax without a legislative supermajority vote.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Karen Fann, argued that Proposition 208's direct funding to schools violates the Education Expenditure Clause and that it unconstitutionally imposes a new tax without the supermajority vote required by the Tax Enactment Clause.
defendant_argument: The defendant, Invest in Arizona, argued that Proposition 208 funds are 'grants' exempt from the Education Expenditure Clause and that the Tax Enactment Clause does not apply to voter initiatives. They also contended the case was not ripe for decision.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the denial of a preliminary injunction against Proposition 208, ruled that the Tax Enactment Clause does not apply to voter initiatives, but found Proposition 208's direct funding unconstitutional to the extent it mandates spending in violation of the Education Expenditure Clause and that these provisions are not severable, remanding the case to the trial court to determine if revenues will exceed the expenditure limit.

title: Redgrave v. Ducey
description: Whether Arizona has consented to damages liability for a state agency's violation of the minimum wage or overtime provisions of the federal Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA).
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the State violated the FLSA by failing to pay minimum wage and overtime, and that Arizona had waived its sovereign immunity to such claims.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that Arizona has not unequivocally consented to federal damages liability under the FLSA, asserting its sovereign immunity.
decision_outcome: The court held that Arizona has not consented to damages liability for a state agency's violation of the FLSA's minimum wage or overtime provisions because the legislature has not expressly or unequivocally implied such consent.

title: State v. Bigger
description: Whether a defendant must present a standard of care expert affidavit to support an ineffective assistance of counsel (IAC) claim, whether Perry v. New Hampshire caused a significant change in Arizona law, and whether A.R.S. § 13-4234(G) supplements rather than conflicts with Arizona Rule of Criminal Procedure 32.4 regarding post-conviction relief filing deadlines.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Ronald Bruce Bigger, argued that he received ineffective assistance of counsel, that Perry v. New Hampshire constituted a significant change in the law entitling him to relief, and that A.R.S. § 13-4234(G) unconstitutionally conflicts with Arizona Rule of Criminal Procedure 32.4.
defendant_argument: The defendant, State of Arizona, argued that Bigger's ineffective assistance of counsel claims were not proven, that Perry v. New Hampshire did not cause a significant change in Arizona law, and implicitly that A.R.S. § 13-4234(G) was constitutional or supplemental to court rules.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the court of appeals' opinion and affirmed the trial court's ruling dismissing Bigger's post-conviction relief petition, finding no expert affidavit is required for IAC claims, Perry did not change Arizona law, and A.R.S. § 13-4234(G) unconstitutionally conflicts with court rules.

title: Mesnard v. Campagnolo
description: Whether a legislator is absolutely immune from liability for defamation when modifying an investigatory report and issuing a news release, under the legislative immunity doctrine.
plaintiff_argument: Mesnard argued he was absolutely immune from defamation liability for both the investigatory report and the news release because these actions constituted legislative functions.
defendant_argument: Shooter argued Mesnard was not immune because his actions, particularly the modifications to the report and the news release, were not legitimate legislative functions and denied due process.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's denial of Mesnard's motion to dismiss regarding the news release, but reversed the denial of dismissal regarding the investigatory report, remanding for further proceedings on the news release claims.

title: State v. Patel
description: Whether A.R.S. § 28-672(G), which limits the amount of restitution for loss resulting from specified traffic offenses, is an unconstitutional limitation on a victim's right to receive full restitution or a valid legislative enactment.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the statutory limitation on restitution was unconstitutional because the Victims' Bill of Rights (VBR) guarantees a victim's right to receive the full amount of restitution for economic loss or injury.
defendant_argument: Patel argued that the plain language of the VBR does not require "full" restitution and that the legislature has the authority to limit the amount of restitution awarded.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that A.R.S. § 28-672(G)'s limitation on restitution is unconstitutional and void, affirming the victim's right to full restitution and reinstating the municipal court's order for $61,191.99.

title: State ex rel. Brnovich v. City of Tucson
description: Whether Arizona Revised Statutes § 16-204.01, which requires political subdivisions to consolidate local elections with state and national elections under certain conditions, can apply to a charter city whose charter mandates off-cycle elections, or if the home rule charter provision precludes such application.
plaintiff_argument: The Attorney General argued that A.R.S. § 16-204.01 should apply to charter cities because increasing voter turnout in local elections is a matter of statewide concern, and low turnout adversely affects the fundamental right to vote and electoral integrity.
defendant_argument: The City of Tucson argued that its home rule charter provision grants it autonomy over purely municipal concerns, including the timing of its local elections, and therefore § 16-204.01 cannot preempt its charter's election-scheduling provisions.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that A.R.S. § 16-204.01 is unconstitutional as applied to the City of Tucson's charter, allowing the city to continue holding off-cycle municipal elections as per its charter and ordinance.

title: Schires v. Carlat
description: Whether the City of Peoria violated the Arizona Constitution's Gift Clause by spending public funds to induce a private university to open a branch campus.
plaintiff_argument: The City's payments to a private university and developer violated the Gift Clause because the public benefits were indirect and the value received by the public was far exceeded by the payments, constituting an impermissible subsidy.
defendant_argument: The City's payments served a public purpose by stimulating economic development and diversifying the economic base, and the value received by the public, including anticipated tax revenue and economic impact, was not far exceeded by the payments.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the lower court's judgment, ruling that the City of Peoria violated the Gift Clause by providing public funds to a private university and developer.

title: State v. Mixton
description: Whether the Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution or article 2, section 8 of the Arizona Constitution requires law enforcement officials to secure a judicially-authorized search warrant or order to obtain a user's Internet Protocol ("IP") address or subscriber information voluntarily provided to an Internet Service Provider ("ISP") as a condition or attribute of service.
plaintiff_argument: Mixton argued that both the Fourth Amendment and article 2, section 8 of the Arizona Constitution require a search warrant or court order to obtain his IP address and ISP subscriber information.
defendant_argument: The State argued that article 2, section 8 of the Arizona Constitution does not require a search warrant or court order for IP addresses and ISP subscriber information, and that the federal third-party doctrine applies.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Mixton's convictions, holding that neither the Fourth Amendment nor article 2, section 8 of the Arizona Constitution requires a search warrant or court order to obtain IP addresses or ISP subscriber information, as this information is not a "private affair" and falls under the third-party doctrine.
